title: How the agent built the MEE-CBC proofs
deck: The saved proposals show concrete proof choices: construct a reduction to CBC, relate the security games, choose invariants for the integrity proof, and break correctness into reusable lemmas. The sections below explain why those choices matter and link them to the completed proofs.

stages.title: Turn a MEE adversary into a CBC adversary
paragraphs: The existing CBC theorem accepts lists of blocks, while a MEE adversary submits messages. The agent proposed MEE_CBCAdv to connect the two: the adapter generates a MAC key, tags and pads each message, then forwards the resulting blocks to the CBC encryption oracle.

The proposal explicitly chooses a direct reduction to CBC. MEE already inlines tagging, padding and encryption, so going through generic composition theorems would require additional program comparisons. The direct route still has to match query limits: pad_tag establishes that the padded length does not depend on the tag, so both games accept the same queries.

This construction makes the existing CBC security bound applicable to MEE. The agent supplies the adapter and the connecting proofs; the switching argument and birthday bound come from the supplied CBC library.
stages.work: Choose a reduction that matches the actual MEE code, and prove that it preserves the query limits.

evidence.text: The reduction adversary: it turns A (an IND$-CPA adversary against the msg-level scheme) into an IND$-CPA adversary against the block-list-level CBC scheme, by owning the MAC key itself and answering A's query p with an oracle query on pad (p, mac mk p).

I deliberately go direct rather than through CPA_CMA/PtE RCPA_preservation: MEE is written inline rather than as MacThenEncrypt(PadThenEncrypt(...),MAC), so routing through those clones would need the same inline-vs-composition equivs plus two extra namespace hops.

stages.title: Separate the two mismatches in the ideal encryption game
paragraphs: The ideal MEE game samples a whole random ciphertext list at once. The CBC theorem uses a procedure that samples its blocks one at a time in a loop. Applying the theorem requires connecting these two programs as well as accounting for the message-to-block conversion.

The agent inserted an intermediate game to separate these issues. Ideal_to_CBCIdeal first relates two whole-list samplers, using pad_tag to show that their list lengths agree. CBCIdeal_to_CBCRandom then uses the existing Random_Ideal equivalence to connect whole-list sampling with the loop. Each lemma handles one mismatch.

The real encryption game has its own comparison of the CBC loops. Two further lemmas match the real- and random-permutation adversaries appearing in the bound. With these relations in place, the final RCPA_security proof rewrites the game probabilities and applies CBC_advantage_bound.
stages.work: Introduce an intermediate game so that ciphertext length and sampling procedure can be proved separately.

evidence.text: First half of the ideal branch, and the easy half: both oracles sample from a single dlist. The model's SKEa was cloned with dC l = dlist d_block (l + 1) and leak m = size (pad (m,witness)); CBCa's SKEa was cloned with dC l = dBlocks (l + 1) = dlist d_block (l + 1) and leak = size. On query p the left samples dlist d_block (size (pad (p,witness)) + 1) and the right dlist d_block (size (pad (p, mac mk p)) + 1); pad_tag makes the two lengths equal, so the oracle case is auto; smt(pad_tag). Splitting the ideal branch here keeps the distribution-shape reasoning apart from the loop-vs-dlist reasoning of the next lemma.

Second half of the ideal branch: CBCa.Conclusion is stated against CBCa.Random (which samples size p + 1 blocks one at a time in a loop), not against CBCa's Ideal (which samples a dlist in one shot). CBCa already exports exactly the bridging equiv `CBCa.Random_Ideal : Random.enc ~ Ideal.enc : size p{1} = size p{2} ==> ={res}`, so this is byequiv; proc; call (_: ={CBCa.OracleBounder.qC, MEE_CBCAdv.mk, glob A}) with the oracle case discharged by call CBCa.Random_Ideal. Both games run the identical adversary, so nothing else moves.

stages.title: Choose the state relation that turns an accepted plaintext into a MAC forgery
paragraphs: For plaintext integrity, the key step is to relate the state of the MEE game to the state of the MAC-forgery game. The proposed invariant matches their encryption and MAC keys, keeps their queried-message sets equal, and requires a MEE win to imply a MAC win. If decryption accepts a new plaintext, its recovered tag must pass the MAC check; verify_oracle_eq makes that implication precise.

The encryption procedures update their query sets at different times. During the CBC loop, one side has already inserted the current message and the other has not. The final enc_oracle_eq proof accounts for this by relating one set plus the current message to the other set, then restoring equality at the procedure boundary.

The decomposition isolates the encryption and verification procedures, lifts both relations through the adversary in forge_eq, and handles key initialization in main_eq. The last step swaps independent key samples to align their order. PTXT_security then follows directly from main_eq.
stages.work: Track keys, query history and the implication between success events, including the different timing of state updates.

evidence.text: The coupling invariant is `PTXT_Wrap.k{1} = (CMAa.ek{2}, WUF_Wrap.k{2}) /\ PTXT_Wrap.s{1} = WUF_Wrap.s{2} /\ (PTXT_Wrap.win{1} => WUF_Wrap.win{2})`. The win implication is the crux: on the left `PTXT_Wrap.verify` sets win when `MEE.dec` returns `Some p'` for an unqueried `p'`, and `MEE.dec` returns `Some p'` exactly when `mac mk p' = t` for the `(p',t)` recovered by `unpad`; on the right `WUF_Wrap.verify` sets win on exactly that same condition. No `mac` reasoning beyond unfolding is needed, and the query set is synchronised because `PTXT_Wrap.enc` adds `p` after the call while `WUF_Wrap.tag` adds it before.

The encryption oracle of the INT-PTXT game and the simulated encryption oracle of the WUF-CMA adversary run the identical CBC loop over `pad (p,t)`; the only differences are where the MAC key is stored and that the queried-message set is updated inside `WUF_Wrap.tag` on the right rather than after the call on the left. Mechanical goal: inline, then one `while` with the loop state matched (`c0{1}=c{2}`, `s{1}=s{2}`, `p'{1}=padded{2}`, `ek{1}=CMAa.ek{2}`).

The whole-game hop, and the only statement the target needs: `byequiv main_eq` closes `PTXT_security` in one tactic. After `call forge_eq` the residual goal is just the key setup — the INT-PTXT game draws the block-cipher key (in `MEE.keygen`) before the MAC key, whereas the WUF game draws the MAC key in `WUF_Wrap.init` and only draws the block-cipher key later inside `CMAa.forge` — so it is discharged by swapping the two independent samplings and `auto`.

stages.title: Make the CBC induction work after the chaining state changes
paragraphs: Decrypting a CBC ciphertext processes the blocks recursively, and each block changes the chaining state used for the next one. The induction hypothesis therefore needs to hold for every chaining state, so it can be applied to the state produced by the current block.

The agent states cbc_encK with the state quantified after the block list. When the proof performs induction on that list, the hypothesis stays general enough for the recursive call. The supporting xorbKl lemma removes the extra XOR with the previous state. In the final proof, cipher inversion, XOR cancellation and the induction hypothesis finish the step.
stages.work: Strengthen the induction statement just enough to cover the changing state in the recursive call.

evidence.text: CBC decryption inverts CBC encryption for every chaining state. The state is quantified after the list so that `elim: p` keeps it generalized, which is exactly what the induction needs (the recursive call runs with st := ci). Uses xorbKl in the cons case.

stages.title: Choose padding lemmas that match the operations in unpad
paragraphs: Undoing the padding requires several facts to fit together. The encoded message contains the message bytes, a 32-byte tag and padding. The proof must recover the bytes from 16-byte blocks, read the padding length from the last byte, and show that the resulting slices recover exactly those three components.

The agent makes the byte/block conversion a separate lemma, with divisibility by 16 as an explicit condition, and proves that the padding rule guarantees it. It also isolates the padding-length range and the last-byte conversion. This lets the remaining proof work with ordinary byte lists.

The slicing lemmas are stated at the indices unpad needs after simplifying its length expressions: size m for the message boundary and size m + 32 for the padding boundary. unpad_cat_pad combines these facts, and unpad_pad specializes them to the chosen padding length. Combining that result with CBC inversion leaves the final mee_correct proof with the check that the recovered tag equals the original tag.
stages.work: Select helper statements that line up with the conversions, guards and slice indices in the decryption code.

evidence.text: Turns every size-dependent index inside unpad into explicit arithmetic: size os - l - 32 = size m and size os - l = size m + 32, which is what the take/drop lemmas below are keyed on.

The octets/blocks round trip: bs2os (os2bs os) = flatten (map ofblock (map mkblock (chunk 16 os))) = flatten (chunk 16 os) = os, by map_ofblockK (with in_chunk_size) then chunkK. This is the bridge that lets all remaining reasoning happen at octet-list level.
Recovers the message component. Pure take_size_cat; stated at index `size m` because size_cat_pad rewrites unpad's `size os - l - 32` to exactly that.
